intro: Oman is one of the oldest independent states in the Arab world. Its sailors once ruled an empire stretching to East Africa.

chapters.title: Frankincense and copper
text: Ancient Oman, called Magan, exported copper to Mesopotamia. In the south, Dhofar grew frankincense, a precious resin burned in temples from Egypt to Rome; the ruins of Sumhuram and Ubar were part of this trade.
Omanis adopted Islam in the 600s, many following the Ibadi school, which is still the main tradition.

chapters.title: A sea empire
text: Portugal seized Muscat in 1507, but the Omanis drove them out in 1650. Oman then built a maritime empire, ruling Zanzibar, Mombasa and parts of the East African coast, and trading with India.
In 1832 the sultan even moved his capital to Zanzibar, which became a separate state in 1861.

highlight.title: Ocean traders
highlight.text: Omani dhows sailed the monsoon winds between Arabia, India and Africa for centuries.

chapters.title: Renaissance
text: By the 1960s Oman was isolated and poor, with only a few kilometres of paved road. In 1970 Sultan Qaboos took power from his father and used oil money to build schools, hospitals and roads, a period called the Renaissance. He ruled until his death in 2020 and was succeeded by Sultan Haitham.
